newsitem.title: UK: Bleak Bulgarian economy frightens off investors.
newsitem.headline: Bleak Bulgarian economy frightens off investors.

text.p: Foreign investors took fright on Tuesday over Bulgaria's increasingly bleak economic outlook after the International Monetary Fund delayed payment of a loan because of Sofia's failure to implement reforms.
Some investment analysts now warn that a Bulgarian default on its debt has become a real risk.
"It's crunch time. If they can't get their act together (and implement IMF reforms) the outlook is very bleak indeed," J.P Morgan economist Mark Thirlwell said.
Prices in the country's Brady bonds -- about the only investment in Bulgaria foreigners are interested in -- have plunged about seven percent in the past two days.
They are now close to their lowest for more than a year.
Behind the sudden loss of confidence is the IMF's decision to postpone payment of the second tranche of a loan, due this month, until Bulgaria makes more economic reforms.
The news comes as Bulgaria, with economic growth sliding, struggles to meet its domestic debt bills, defend a fast-falling currency and stop inflation from surging any higher.
The Fund promised earlier this year to help out Bulgaria as long as it shut down scores of loss-making state companies and kept monetary policy under control.
Bulgaria's failure to meet those targets now means a delay in new IMF payments until October at the earliest, analysts said.
"It's hard to be very optimistic. It is looking to me as though they are blowing the last chance they have," said Chase Manhattan International analyst Robin Hubbard.

Though he expected Bulgaria would eventually do enough for the IMF to release the $115 million payment, doubts still hung over how it would pick up enough foreign exchange to meet next year's debt servicing payments.
"We can't take for granted that the IMF is going to continue to bankroll Bulgaria...they have to aggressively adhere to the requirements of the IMF," said Salomon Brothers analyst David Boren.

October's presidential election only makes it harder for the government to implement very unpopular reforms in the impoverished country which already lags much of the rest of the old East Bloc in the transition to a market economy, analysts said.
"It is politically costly in the short-term to go ahead with the reforms but ultimately the economic costs of not doing so would be far larger," said J.P. Morgan's Thirlwell.
But some analysts take heart in the fact that at least the IMF is still pressing Bulgaria to make the necessary sacrifices it needs to bring growth and prevent economic collapse.
"The IMF needs to get maximum pressure on the government..I honestly do not not think Bulgaria is going to be allowed to default," ANZ economist Jerome Booth said.
One positive sign was that the price of Bulgarian Brady bonds, after going into near free-fall, did eventually start to recover a little by Tuesday afternoon.
Its huge yield compared to almost any other emerging market debt, still makes it irresistable to some investors prepared to take the risk, one trader said.
